system: You are a staff engineer who summarises technical discussions into decisions. Be neutral between positions.
turns:
Summarise this RFC thread: what's proposed, the main objections, where people agree, and what remains to be decided. Then say what decision you think the group is converging on.

RFC: API versioning strategy for the public REST API

Proposal (Imogen). Today we version in the URL path: /v1/, /v2/. We've had v2 for three years and are afraid to make v3 because of the migration cost to customers, so breaking changes pile up as awkward optional parameters. I propose date-based versions sent in a header. Each account is pinned to the API version current when it first made a request. Breaking changes ship behind a new dated version; internally we keep a chain of small transformation layers that convert responses from the newest shape back to older ones. Customers upgrade by changing one header when they're ready, and can test by overriding it per request.

Comment (Rafael). I like not having big-bang versions. My worry is the transformation chain. After three years we could have forty layers and a response passing through all of them. Who tests every combination? I'd want a hard rule that versions older than 24 months are retired.

Comment (Imogen). Agreed on a retirement window. On testing: each layer has its own tests, and we replay recorded traffic against old versions in CI.

Comment (Sung-min, developer relations). From the customer side, headers are less discoverable than a path. People paste URLs into browsers and chat. Half our support tickets are from people who aren't professional developers. I'd want the version visible in the dashboard, echoed in every response header, and included in error messages. Also our docs need to render per version, which they can't today.

Comment (Abena, SDK team). SDKs make this mostly invisible: each SDK release pins the version it was built for. But that means an SDK upgrade becomes an API upgrade, and people will be surprised. We need a changelog that's generated from the same source as the transformation layers, or they will drift.

Comment (Rafael). What counts as breaking? Adding a field isn't. Adding an enum value arguably is, because strict clients crash. We need a written policy before any of this.

Comment (Lucia, security). Pinning per account means a security fix that changes behaviour can't reach pinned customers. I need an explicit carve-out: security-relevant changes apply to all versions.

Comment (Imogen). Yes to the security carve-out and to a written breaking-change policy; I'll draft both. On discoverability I accept the costs Sung-min lists; I think they're one-off.

Comment (Dmitri, engineering manager). I'm supportive but not of doing this and the billing rework in the same half. Can we trial it on one new resource first, say the upcoming webhooks endpoints, keep /v2/ as is, and decide on full adoption after two quarters?

Comment (Sung-min). A trial on new endpoints only means two versioning schemes at once in the docs. That's confusing, but less risky. I can live with it if the trial has an end date.

Comment (Abena). Fine with the trial. I need eight weeks' notice before anything ships to prepare the SDKs.
Write the 'Decision' section as it might appear in the final RFC, clearly marking anything you had to assume.
Which objection do you think was answered least convincingly?

Summarise in five bullet points for a parent newsletter, staying neutral.

A secondary school in the coastal town of Port Aldwin will keep its ban on mobile phones during the school day after a year-long trial that teachers say has changed the atmosphere in classrooms and corridors, though the evidence on academic results remains thin and some students and parents are unconvinced.

Under the policy, introduced last February, the school's 840 students place their phones in lockable fabric pouches at the gate each morning and unlock them at a station on the way out. Smartwatches with messaging functions are covered too. Students who need a phone for medical reasons, such as glucose monitoring, are exempt.

The principal told a meeting of about a hundred parents on Wednesday that recorded incidents of bullying during school hours had fallen from 61 in the year before the trial to 38, and that confiscations, previously running at several a day, had 'essentially stopped because there is nothing to confiscate'. Library borrowing rose by a third. A staff survey found 88 percent of teachers wanted the ban to continue.

A student survey was more mixed. Just over half of respondents said they found it easier to concentrate, and a similar share said lunchtimes were 'more social'. But 41 percent said the ban made them more anxious, most commonly because they could not contact a parent or check on a part-time job roster. Several senior students said the rule treated seventeen-year-olds the same as twelve-year-olds.

On academic outcomes, the principal was cautious. Mid-year test results were slightly higher than the previous year's, she said, but 'one year, one school, and a different group of students' made it impossible to credit the phone policy.

Some parents objected to the cost: the pouches are leased at 22 dollars per student per year, paid from the school's discretionary budget. One father said the money would be better spent on a counsellor. Another parent asked what would happen in an emergency; the principal said the office could reach any student within minutes and that staff could unlock pouches in a lockdown.

The school council voted to continue the policy for a further two years, with a review of the rule for final-year students to be completed by the end of term.
Now a version for the student newspaper, 100 words, that takes the students' concerns seriously.
What numbers would you want to see before concluding the ban 'worked'?

system: You are a technical writer for a help centre. Use numbered steps, one action per step, and bold the names of buttons.
turns:
This article was written by one of our engineers. Customers keep getting lost in it. Rewrite it as a clean how-to with prerequisites, steps and troubleshooting.

Setting up automatic bank feeds

So basically bank feeds let transactions come in automatically rather than you uploading statement files, which is obviously better. Before you start you should know that not all banks are supported, there is a list in settings, and also you need to be an admin or at least have the 'banking' permission, otherwise the button won't be there, which a lot of people ask about. Also it only works for accounts in the same currency as your organisation's base currency at the moment.

Go to Accounting then Bank accounts and find the account you want. If you haven't added the account yet you need to do that first using Add account and entering the account name and number. Then click the three dots on the account tile and choose Connect feed, or if you're on the new layout it's a Connect button directly on the tile. You'll get a popup listing banks. Pick yours. You then get sent to your bank's own site to log in, we never see your banking password. Your bank will ask which accounts to share, tick the right one(s), and approve. Some banks then send a code by text. After that you get bounced back to us.

Now the bit that confuses people: you have to choose a start date for importing. If you've already imported statements by hand up to, say, the 10th, pick the 11th, otherwise you'll get duplicates and have to delete them one by one, because bulk delete isn't available for feed transactions. If you don't know, check the last transaction date in the account's Transactions tab before you do any of this. Honestly do that first.

Then click Finish. The first import can take up to an hour, sometimes longer for business accounts with a lot of history. After that transactions come in once a day, usually overnight. They show up under the Reconcile tab.

Things that go wrong. If the feed says 'Action required' after a few months that's because banks make you re-approve access every 90 days or so; click Renew and log in to your bank again. If you connected the wrong account, disconnect from the three dots menu, which keeps the transactions already imported. If nothing has come in after 24 hours contact support and tell us the bank and the last four digits of the account. Joint accounts sometimes need both holders to approve, depending on the bank.
Add a short 'Before you begin' checklist at the top with exactly four items.

Our CEO sent this to all staff. Give me three versions of a summary: one sentence, three bullets, and a paragraph for the engineering team focused only on what affects them.

Subject: Where we are after Q3

Hi everyone,

I want to share where we stand after the third quarter, plainly, including the parts that aren't comfortable.

Revenue for the quarter came in at 4.1 million, up 9 percent on Q2 but about 6 percent short of our plan. The gap is almost entirely in new enterprise deals: we expected to close five and closed two. The three that slipped are not lost, but two of them are now waiting on the single sign-on and audit log features we've been promising since spring. Self-serve revenue, on the other hand, beat plan by 14 percent, helped by the simplified pricing page and the new onboarding flow. Thank you to the growth team for that.

Churn rose slightly, from 1.8 to 2.3 percent monthly among small customers. When we asked people why they left, the most common answer by far was reliability. We had four significant outages this quarter against one in Q2. I know how hard the infrastructure team has worked, and I also know they've been asking for time to pay down the causes for most of the year. They were right and I should have listened sooner.

So here is what changes in Q4. First, reliability becomes the top engineering priority. For the next eight weeks, half of all engineering time goes to the stability backlog, and no new feature work will be scheduled that conflicts with it. Second, the one exception is the enterprise pair, single sign-on and audit logs, which a dedicated group of four will deliver by 15 December. Third, everything else on the roadmap, including the mobile redesign and the marketplace, moves into next year. I know several of you have put a lot into those and this will be disappointing.

On costs: we are not planning layoffs. We are pausing hiring for all roles except two site reliability engineers and one enterprise support specialist. Travel is limited to customer visits. We have 19 months of runway at current spend, and I'd like to end the year with at least 18.

The all-hands on Thursday will be entirely questions and answers. Send questions ahead anonymously if you prefer; I'll answer all of them, including the pointed ones.

Thank you for the work, and for your patience with me.

Marisol
